spatial_claims.claim: Cylinder has axis AB; cutting plane meets AB at point C, so C lies on segment AB
Cutting plane is parallel to both base planes of the cylinder
K is a cylinder with axis AC and L is a cylinder with axis CB, both with the same base radius as the original
M and N are points on a ray extending beyond A, with AM = m·AC and AN = n·CB
m congruent copies of K assembled consecutively along AM from base at A, forming cylinder X with axis AM
n congruent copies of L assembled consecutively along AN from same base at A, forming cylinder Y with axis AN
X and Y have the same radius (inherited from K and L)
X and Y share the same starting base, same axis ray, and same radius; if AM > AN then Y is a proper part of X
If AM < AN then X is a proper part of Y; if AM = AN they coincide

configuration_map: All points A, B, C, M, N are collinear on the cylinder's axis or its extension. C lies between A and B, partitioning axis AB into AC and CB. M and N lie on the ray from A extending beyond A (away from B), at distances AM = m·AC and AN = n·CB respectively. Cylinders K (axis AC) and L (axis CB) have the same base radius r. Cylinder X (m copies of K, axis AM, radius r) and cylinder Y (n copies of L, axis AN, radius r) both start from the base at A along the same ray. The entire configuration is one-dimensional along the axis, extended to 3D by uniform rotation with constant radius. No non-collinear point relationships or angle decompositions arise.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The configuration is purely collinear (points along a single axis), and all cylinders share the same radius and axis direction. The containment/equality comparisons in Step 4 follow correctly from the construction. No angle decompositions, interior/exterior claims, or competing betweenness relationships arise. The proof uses a different path from Heath (rotational definitions and coincidence rather than 12.11) but the geometric reasoning is internally sound.
